question.stem: An engineer connects to MongoDB, runs `use inventoryDB`, and immediately executes `show dbs` without inserting records; what appears regarding `inventoryDB`?

options.A: `inventoryDB` is omitted from `show dbs` because no collection data has been written yet
options.B: `inventoryDB` appears with a reserved size of `1.000GB`
options.C: `show dbs` throws a fatal catalog exception until `db.createCollection()` runs
options.D: `inventoryDB` replaces `local` in the default server output

answer.explanation: A database selected via `use <databaseName>` only appears in `show dbs` once it actually holds data on disk. Until a document or collection is written, `inventoryDB` remains in memory only and is excluded from `show dbs`. (Key Takeaway: Unwritten databases selected with `use` remain hidden from `show dbs`.)

question.stem: If a session switches to `tempDB` via `use tempDB` and executes `db.logs.insertOne({ msg: "boot" })`, which objects are auto-created?

options.A: Only the `logs` collection is created; `tempDB` must pre-exist
options.B: Neither `tempDB` nor `logs` is created without `db.createCollection("logs")`
options.C: Both the `tempDB` database on disk and the `logs` collection are created automatically
options.D: Only the `tempDB` database is created; the document is discarded

answer.explanation: When `insertOne()` runs against a non-existent collection in a newly selected database, MongoDB automatically creates the `logs` collection and simultaneously materializes the `tempDB` database on disk. (Key Takeaway: First document insertion auto-creates both the missing collection and its parent database.)

question.stem: Which query retrieves all student documents where `age` is at least `18` and projects strictly `name` and `age` while omitting `_id`?

options.A: `db.students.find({ age: { $gt: 18 } }, { name: 1, age: 1 })`
options.B: `db.students.find({ age: { $gte: 18 } }, { name: 1, age: 1, _id: 0 })`
options.C: `db.students.find({ age: { $lte: 18 } }, { name: 0, age: 0, _id: 1 })`
options.D: `db.students.findOne({ age: { $gte: 18 } }).sort({ age: 1 })`

answer.explanation: `$gte: 18` filters for `age` greater than or equal to 18, and the projection `{ name: 1, age: 1, _id: 0 }` includes `name` and `age` while explicitly suppressing `_id` (which is otherwise returned by default). (Key Takeaway: Combine `{ $gte: 18 }` in the filter with `{ name: 1, age: 1, _id: 0 }` in the projection.)

question.stem: A collection stores 50 student documents; how many documents are emitted by `db.students.find().sort({ age: 1 }).skip(10).limit(5)`?

options.A: 10 documents starting from the 5th youngest student
options.B: 15 documents ordered from oldest to youngest
options.C: 40 documents after removing the first 10 matches
options.D: 5 documents representing the 11th through 15th students in ascending `age` order

answer.explanation: `sort({ age: 1 })` orders documents in ascending order of `age`, `skip(10)` omits the first 10 results (positions 1–10), and `limit(5)` caps the output to the next 5 documents (positions 11–15). (Key Takeaway: `sort(1).skip(10).limit(5)` returns items 11 through 15 in ascending order.)

question.stem: Why does executing `db.students.findOne({ grade: 8 }).sort({ name: 1 })` fail at runtime in the MongoDB shell?

options.A: Because `findOne()` returns a single document object (or `null`) rather than a cursor, so cursor methods like `sort()` cannot be chained on it
options.B: Because `sort()` only accepts `-1` and rejects `1` as a sort direction
options.C: Because `findOne()` forbids equality filters on numeric fields such as `grade`
options.D: Because `sort()` must be passed inside the second projection parameter of `findOne()`

answer.explanation: Unlike `find()`, which returns a cursor supporting `.sort()`, `.limit()`, and `.skip()`, `findOne()` resolves immediately to a single document object (or `null`) and does not support cursor methods directly. (Key Takeaway: `findOne()` returns a document rather than a cursor and cannot chain `.sort()` or `.limit()`.)

question.stem: Which filter expression matches students whose `age` is either `17`, `18`, or `19` without writing multiple `$or` clauses?

answer.explanation: The `$in` operator matches documents where the field value equals any element in the specified array (`{ age: { $in: [17, 18, 19] } }`). `$nin` excludes those values, and `$gt: 17, $lt: 19` would only match `18`. (Key Takeaway: Use `$in` with an array of target values for concise set-membership filtering.)

question.stem: What is the exact state change on Rahul's document `{ name: "Rahul", age: 19, attempts: 2, subjects: ["Math", "Science"] }` after running `db.students.updateOne({ name: "Rahul" }, { $set: { age: 20 }, $inc: { attempts: 1 }, $push: { subjects: "History" } })`?

options.A: `age` becomes `39`, `attempts` becomes `1`, and `subjects` is replaced by `"History"`
options.B: `age` becomes `20`, `attempts` becomes `3`, and `"History"` is appended to `subjects`
options.C: `age` remains `19`, `attempts` becomes `3`, and `"Science"` is removed from `subjects`
options.D: A new document is inserted because `$set`, `$inc`, and `$push` cannot be combined

answer.explanation: In a single `updateOne` call, `$set: { age: 20 }` replaces `age` with `20`, `$inc: { attempts: 1 }` increments `attempts` from `2` to `3`, and `$push: { subjects: "History" }` appends `"History"` to the `subjects` array. (Key Takeaway: `$set`, `$inc`, and `$push` can be combined atomically in a single update document.)

question.stem: Four documents in `students` have `{ age: 18 }`; how do `updateOne({ age: 18 }, { $set: { promoted: true } })` and `updateMany({ age: 18 }, { $set: { promoted: true } })` compare?

options.A: Both commands update all four matching documents identically
options.B: `updateOne` throws an exception when more than one document matches `{ age: 18 }`
options.C: `updateOne` modifies only the first matching document, whereas `updateMany` modifies all four matching documents
options.D: `updateOne` replaces the entire document, whereas `updateMany` modifies only the `promoted` field

answer.explanation: `updateOne(filter, update)` updates strictly the first document that matches the filter, leaving the other three `{ age: 18 }` documents unchanged, whereas `updateMany(filter, update)` applies `{ $set: { promoted: true } }` to every matching document. (Key Takeaway: `updateOne()` mutates the first match only; `updateMany()` mutates all matches.)

question.stem: Which update command removes every instance of `"Science"` from Rahul's `subjects` array field without altering other array elements?

options.A: `db.students.updateOne({ name: "Rahul" }, { $pull: { subjects: "Science" } })`
options.B: `db.students.updateOne({ name: "Rahul" }, { $push: { subjects: "Science" } })`
options.C: `db.students.deleteOne({ name: "Rahul", subjects: "Science" })`
options.D: `db.students.updateOne({ name: "Rahul" }, { $inc: { subjects: -1 } })`

answer.explanation: The `$pull` update operator removes matching values (`"Science"`) from an existing array field (`subjects`), whereas `$push` appends elements and `deleteOne` would delete Rahul's entire document. (Key Takeaway: `$pull` removes specified elements from an array field in place.)

question.stem: If three documents in `students` have `{ grade: 7 }`, what is the outcome of executing `db.students.deleteOne({ grade: 7 })`?

options.A: All three documents with `{ grade: 7 }` are permanently deleted
options.B: No documents are deleted because the filter is non-unique
options.C: The entire `students` collection is dropped from the database
options.D: Strictly the first document matching `{ grade: 7 }` is deleted, while the remaining two stay in the collection

answer.explanation: `deleteOne(filter)` deletes only the first document that matches the query filter `{ grade: 7 }`, leaving the remaining two matching documents intact. Deleting all three requires `deleteMany({ grade: 7 })`. (Key Takeaway: `deleteOne()` removes only the first matching document.)
